problems.title: Business card
problems.description:
# Lecture 01 · Homework 01 · Business card

## Task

Print your **name**, your **class** and a **favourite quote** inside a box drawn with `*`.

- Use the tab character `\t` to line up the values after `Name:` and `Class:`.
- The quote must be printed with real quotation marks, using `\"`.
- The right border of the box must be a straight line.

## Input

None.

## Output

Five lines: the top border, the name line, the class line, the quote line and the bottom border.

## Example

Output:

```
**********************************
*  Name:        Ana Petrova      *
*  Class:       III-2            *
*  "Code is poetry"              *
**********************************
```

(`Name:` and `Class:` are followed by a tab, which the console shows as spaces up to column 16.)

## Hints

1. Write one `cout` for every line of the box.
2. `\t` is **one** character. It moves the cursor to the next multiple of 8 columns (8, 16, 24, ...).
3. Inside a string, `\"` prints `"` instead of ending the string.
4. Count the characters so the right `*` of every line is in the same column (column 34).

## Extra challenge

Put your own name, class and quote in the card, and keep the right border straight.

problems.title: Echo and greet
problems.description:
# Lecture 01 · Homework 02 · Echo and greet

## Task

Read a first name and an age, and print how old the person will be in 10 years.

## Input

One line: a first name (one word, no spaces) and an age (a whole number, 0 to 120).

## Output

`Hi NAME, in 10 years you will be AGE.` where AGE is the age plus 10.

## Example

| Input | Output |
|---|---|
| `Marko 15` | `Hi Marko, in 10 years you will be 25.` |
| `Ana 9` | `Hi Ana, in 10 years you will be 19.` |

## Hints

1. `cin >> name >> age;` reads both values.
2. You can write `age + 10` directly inside `cout`.
3. Watch the spaces inside the quotes.

tests.output: Hi Marko, in 10 years you will be 25.
Hi Ana, in 10 years you will be 19.

problems.title: Rectangle calculator
problems.description:
# Lecture 01 · Homework 03 · Rectangle calculator ## Task Read the width and the height of a rectangle and print its area and its perimeter with exactly 2 decimals. ## Input One line: two positive numbers, the width and the height (decimals allowed). ## Output Two lines: `Area: A` and `Perimeter: P`, both with exactly 2 decimals. ## Example | Input | Output | |---|---| | `3.5 2` | `Area: 7.00`
`Perimeter: 11.00` | | `10 4.25` | `Area: 42.50`
`Perimeter: 28.50` | | `1.333 3` | `Area: 4.00`
`Perimeter: 8.67` | ## Hints 1. Use `double`, not `int`, so that `3.5` keeps its decimal part. 2. The perimeter is `2 * (width + height)`. The parentheses matter. 3. `cout << fixed << setprecision(2);` needs `#include `.

problems.title: Circle with const
problems.description:
# Lecture 01 · Homework 04 · Circle with const ## Task Define `const double PI = 3.14159;`. Read the radius of a circle and print its area and its circumference. ## Input One positive number `r`, the radius (decimals allowed). ## Output Two lines: `Area: A` where A = PI · r · r, and `Circumference: C` where C = 2 · PI · r. Print the numbers with plain `cout` (default format). ## Example | Input | Output | |---|---| | `3` | `Area: 28.2743`
`Circumference: 18.8495` | | `10` | `Area: 314.159`
`Circumference: 62.8318` | | `1` | `Area: 3.14159`
`Circumference: 6.28318` | ## Hints 1. `const` goes before the type: `const double PI = 3.14159;` 2. There is no squared operator: write `r * r`. (`^` does something else in C++.) 3. Try writing `PI = 3;` after the definition and read the compiler error.

problems.title: Seconds converter
problems.description:
# Lecture 01 · Homework 05 · Seconds converter

## Task

Read a number of seconds and print it as hours, minutes and seconds.

## Input

One whole number, 0 to 86399 (less than one day).

## Output

`H h M min S s`, where M and S are between 0 and 59.

## Example

| Input | Output |
|---|---|
| `3725` | `1 h 2 min 5 s` |
| `86399` | `23 h 59 min 59 s` |
| `59` | `0 h 0 min 59 s` |

## Hints

1. `3725 / 3600` is `1`: dividing two `int`s drops the decimal part.
2. `3725 % 3600` is `125`: the seconds left after the full hours.
3. Compute the minutes from the leftover, not from the total.

problems.title: Digit splitter
problems.description:
# Lecture 01 · Homework 06 · Digit splitter ## Task Read a 3-digit number. Print each digit on its own line, then the sum of the digits. ## Input One whole number from 100 to 999. ## Output Four lines: the hundreds digit, the tens digit, the ones digit, and `Sum: S`. ## Example | Input | Output | |---|---| | `482` | `4`
`8`
`2`
`Sum: 14` | | `905` | `9`
`0`
`5`
`Sum: 14` | | `100` | `1`
`0`
`0`
`Sum: 1` | ## Hints 1. `n % 10` is the last digit. 2. `n / 10` removes the last digit (482 becomes 48). 3. The middle digit is `n / 10 % 10`, the first digit is `n / 100`.

problems.title: Reverse a 4-digit number
problems.description:
# Lecture 01 · Homework 07 · Reverse a 4-digit number

## Task

Read a 4-digit number and print it reversed, using only `%` and `/` (no loops, no strings).

## Input

One whole number from 1000 to 9999.

## Output

The reversed number as an `int`. Leading zeros disappear: `1200` prints `21`.

## Example

| Input | Output |
|---|---|
| `1234` | `4321` |
| `1200` | `21` |
| `9071` | `1709` |

## Hints

1. The digits are `n / 1000`, `n / 100 % 10`, `n / 10 % 10` and `n % 10`.
2. The reversed number is `d4 * 1000 + d3 * 100 + d2 * 10 + d1`.
3. Why does `1200` give `21`? Think about what `0 * 1000` adds.

problems.title: Even / odd and sign
problems.description:
# Lecture 01 · Homework 08 · Even / odd and sign

## Task

Read an integer. Print whether it is even or odd, and whether it is positive, negative or zero.

## Input

One whole number (it can be negative).

## Output

One line: `even` or `odd`, then `, positive`, `, negative` or `, zero`.

## Example

| Input | Output |
|---|---|
| `-7` | `odd, negative` |
| `0` | `even, zero` |
| `12` | `even, positive` |

## Hints

1. A number is even when `n % 2 == 0`.
2. Careful: `-7 % 2` is `-1` in C++, so `n % 2 == 1` misses negative odd numbers.
3. Use `if`, `else if`, `else` for the three sign cases.

problems.title: Max of three
problems.description:
# Lecture 01 · Homework 09 · Max of three ## Task Read three integers and print the largest. Solve it twice: (a) with `if / else` only, (b) with `max(max(a, b), c)`. Print both answers so you can see that they agree. ## Input One line: three whole numbers `a b c` (they can be negative or equal). ## Output Two lines: `if/else: X` and `max: X`, where X is the largest number. ## Example | Input | Output | |---|---| | `4 9 2` | `if/else: 9`
`max: 9` | | `-5 -2 -8` | `if/else: -2`
`max: -2` | | `7 3 7` | `if/else: 7`
`max: 7` | ## Hints 1. `a` is the largest if `a >= b && a >= c`. Otherwise compare only `b` and `c`. 2. Do not write `a > b && c`: that means `(a > b) && (c != 0)`. 3. `max` needs `#include `.

problems.title: Grade converter
problems.description:
# Lecture 01 · Homework 10 · Grade converter

## Task

Read points and print the grade: 0-49 → 5, 50-64 → 6, 65-74 → 7, 75-84 → 8, 85-94 → 9, 95-100 → 10. Anything outside 0-100 prints `Invalid`.

## Input

One whole number (it may be outside 0-100).

## Output

The grade (5 to 10), or `Invalid`.

## Example

| Input | Output |
|---|---|
| `78` | `8` |
| `120` | `Invalid` |
| `95` | `10` |

## Hints

1. Check `points < 0 || points > 100` first.
2. Then go from the highest grade down: `>= 95`, `>= 85`, `>= 75`, ...
3. In an `else if` chain only the first true branch runs, so you do not need upper limits.

problems.title: Leap year
problems.description:
# Lecture 01 · Homework 11 · Leap year

## Task

Read a year and print whether it is a leap year. Rule: divisible by 4 and not by 100, OR divisible by 400. Write the condition as one expression.

## Input

One whole number, the year (1 to 9999).

## Output

`leap` or `not leap`.

## Example

| Input | Output |
|---|---|
| `2024` | `leap` |
| `1900` | `not leap` |
| `2000` | `leap` |

## Hints

1. Divisible by 4: `year % 4 == 0`. Not divisible by 100: `year % 100 != 0`.
2. `(A && B) || C`: the parentheses make the meaning clear.
3. Use `==` to compare. A single `=` is an assignment and will not compile here.

problems.title: Triangle checker
problems.description:
# Lecture 01 · Homework 12 · Triangle checker

## Task

Read three side lengths. Print whether they can form a triangle: every side must be shorter than the sum of the other two. If they can, print what kind of triangle it is.

## Input

One line: three whole numbers `a b c` (1 to 1000), the side lengths.

## Output

One word or phrase:
- `no triangle` if the sides cannot form a triangle,
- `equilateral` if all three sides are equal,
- `isosceles` if exactly two sides are equal,
- `scalene` if all three sides are different.

## Example

| Input | Output |
|---|---|
| `3 4 5` | `scalene` |
| `2 2 2` | `equilateral` |
| `1 2 5` | `no triangle` |

## Hints

1. "Not a triangle" is easier to write: `a + b <= c || a + c <= b || b + c <= a`.
2. Use one `if / else if / else` chain. The first true condition wins.
3. Check `equilateral` before `isosceles`: three equal sides also have two equal sides!

problems.title: Char explorer
problems.description:
# Lecture 01 · Homework 13 · Char explorer

## Task

Read one character. Print its ASCII code, and say whether it is a digit, an uppercase letter, a lowercase letter, or something else.

## Input

One character (not a space).

## Output

`CODE, KIND` where CODE is the ASCII code of the character and KIND is one of `digit`, `uppercase letter`, `lowercase letter`, `other`.

## Example

| Input | Output |
|---|---|
| `g` | `103, lowercase letter` |
| `7` | `55, digit` |
| `#` | `35, other` |

## Hints

1. `(int)c` gives the number behind the character `c`.
2. A range check needs two comparisons joined with `&&`: `'a' <= c && c <= 'z'`.
3. Use single quotes for a character: `'a'`, not `"a"`.

problems.title: Case flipper
problems.description:
# Lecture 01 · Homework 14 · Case flipper

## Task

Read one letter and print it in the opposite case: a lowercase letter becomes uppercase, an uppercase letter becomes lowercase. Use only arithmetic on `char` (no `toupper` / `tolower`).

## Input

One English letter, `a`-`z` or `A`-`Z`.

## Output

The same letter in the opposite case.

## Example

| Input | Output |
|---|---|
| `a` | `A` |
| `Q` | `q` |
| `m` | `M` |

## Hints

1. Letters are numbers: `'a'` is 97, `'A'` is 65.
2. `c - 'a'` is the position of a lowercase letter in the alphabet (0 for `a`).
3. `c = c - 'a' + 'A';` moves it to the uppercase row. Store the result back in a `char` before printing, otherwise `cout` prints a number.

problems.title: Overflow detective
problems.description:
# Lecture 01 · Homework 15 · Overflow detective ## Task (a) Store `INT_MAX` (the biggest `int`) in an `int` and add 1. (b) Read a big number and store it in an `int`. Print both results and look at what happened. Then fix both with `long long`. ## Input One whole number bigger than `INT_MAX`, for example `5000000000` (read it into a `long long`). ## Output Three lines: ``` int: 2147483647 + 1 = X int: BIG -> Y long long: 2147483648 and BIG ``` where X and Y are the values the `int` variables really hold. ## Example | Input | Output | |---|---| | `5000000000` | `int: 2147483647 + 1 = -2147483648`
`int: 5000000000 -> 705032704`
`long long: 2147483648 and 5000000000` | ## Hints 1. `#include ` gives you `INT_MAX`. 2. An `int` has 4 bytes, a `long long` has 8 bytes. 3. `long long y = INT_MAX + 1;` still overflows: the sum is computed in `int` first. Store `INT_MAX` in the `long long` first, then add 1.

problems.title: Float trap
problems.description:
# Lecture 01 · Homework 16 · Float trap ## Task Read three decimal numbers `a`, `b`, `c`. Print `a + b` and `c` with 17 significant digits. Then print whether `a + b == c`, and whether they are equal using the safe comparison `abs(a + b - c) < 1e-9`. ## Input One line: three decimal numbers `a b c`. ## Output Four lines: ``` a + b = SUM c = C equal? true/false safe equal? true/false ``` ## Example | Input | Output | |---|---| | `0.1 0.2 0.3` | `a + b = 0.30000000000000004`
`c = 0.29999999999999999`
`equal? false`
`safe equal? true` | | `0.5 0.25 0.75` | `a + b = 0.75`
`c = 0.75`
`equal? true`
`safe equal? true` | ## Hints 1. `#include ` for `setprecision(17)`, `#include ` for `abs`. 2. `cout << boolalpha;` prints `true` / `false` instead of `1` / `0`. 3. Never compare two `double` values with `==`: check that their difference is tiny.

tests.output:
a + b = 0.75
c     = 0.75
equal? true
safe equal? true

problems.title: Distance and rounding
problems.description:
# Lecture 01 · Homework 17 · Distance and rounding ## Task Read two points (x1, y1) and (x2, y2). Print the distance between them, then the same distance rounded with `ceil`, `floor` and `round`. ## Input One line: four numbers `x1 y1 x2 y2`. ## Output Four lines: ``` D ceil C floor F round R ``` D is printed with the default `cout` precision (6 significant digits). ## Example | Input | Output | |---|---| | `0 0 3 5` | `5.83095`
`ceil 6`
`floor 5`
`round 6` | | `1 1 4 5` | `5`
`ceil 5`
`floor 5`
`round 5` | ## Hints 1. Pythagoras: `d = sqrt(dx*dx + dy*dy)` where `dx = x2 - x1` and `dy = y2 - y1`. 2. `^` is not "power" in C++. Use `pow(dx, 2)` or `dx * dx`. 3. `ceil` rounds up, `floor` rounds down, `round` goes to the nearest whole number. All need `#include `.

problems.title: Quadratic equation
problems.description:
# Lecture 01 · Homework 18 · Quadratic equation

## Task

Read the coefficients `a`, `b`, `c` of the equation a·x² + b·x + c = 0 (a is not 0). Compute the discriminant D = b² − 4ac and print the real roots.

## Input

One line: three whole numbers `a b c`, with `a != 0`.

## Output

- If D > 0: `X1 and X2` where X1 = (−b + √D) / 2a and X2 = (−b − √D) / 2a.
- If D = 0: the single root −b / 2a.
- If D < 0: `no real roots`.

## Example

| Input | Output |
|---|---|
| `1 -3 2` | `2 and 1` |
| `1 2 1` | `-1` |
| `1 0 1` | `no real roots` |

## Hints

1. `double D = pow(b, 2) - 4 * a * c;`
2. Brackets matter: `(-b + sqrt(D)) / (2 * a)`, not `-b + sqrt(D) / 2 * a`.
3. Check the sign of D before calling `sqrt`: the square root of a negative number is not a real number.

problems.title: Function practice
problems.description:
# Lecture 01 · Homework 19 · Function practice ## Task Write three functions and call each of them twice from `main`: - `int cube(int x)` returns `x * x * x`, - `bool isDivisible(int a, int b)` returns `true` if `a % b == 0`, - `void printLine(int length)` prints `length` dashes `-` and ends the line. `main` reads two numbers `a` and `b` and prints: 1. `cube(a)` and `cube(b)`, separated by a space, 2. `isDivisible(a, b)` and `isDivisible(b, a)`, as `true` / `false`, 3. `printLine(a)`, 4. `printLine(b)`. ## Input One line: two whole numbers `a b` (1 to 100). ## Output Four lines, as described above. ## Example | Input | Output | |---|---| | `6 3` | `216 27`
`true false`
`------`
`---` | | `4 8` | `64 512`
`false true`
`----`
`--------` | ## Hints 1. Write the functions above `main`, so `main` already knows them. 2. `string(length, '-')` builds a string of `length` dashes (`#include `). 3. A `void` function returns nothing: call it on its own line, not inside `cout`.

problems.title: Complexity audit
Countdown to launch
problems.description:
# Lecture 02 · Homework 01 · Countdown to launch ## Task Read a whole number N and count down to the launch: print N, N-1, ..., 1 on one line, followed by `Liftoff!`. Write the countdown twice: once with a `for` loop and once with a `while` loop (so the line is printed two times). ## Input One whole number N (0 to 100). ## Output Two identical lines: the numbers from N down to 1, each followed by a space, and then `Liftoff!`. ## Example | Input | Output | |---|---| | `5` | `5 4 3 2 1 Liftoff!`
`5 4 3 2 1 Liftoff!` | | `0` | `Liftoff!`
`Liftoff!` | ## Hints 1. `for (int i = n; i >= 1; i--)` counts down from n to 1. 2. In the `while` version the start (`int i = n;`) goes before the loop and the step (`i--;`) is the last line of the body. 3. Print `Liftoff!` after the loop, not inside it. 4. If you forget `i--` in the `while` loop, it never stops.

problems.title: Multiplication table
problems.description:
# Lecture 02 · Homework 02 · Multiplication table ## Task Read a whole number n and print its multiplication table from 1 to 10. ## Input One whole number n (-1000 to 1000). ## Output Ten lines. Line i (from 1 to 10) is `n x i = RESULT`, where RESULT is n multiplied by i. ## Example | Input | Output | |---|---| | `7` | `7 x 1 = 7`
`7 x 2 = 14`
`...`
`7 x 10 = 70` | | `0` | `0 x 1 = 0`
`...`
`0 x 10 = 0` | ## Hints 1. `for (int i = 1; i <= 10; i++)` gives exactly 10 passes. 2. Use `i` inside the body: `cout << n << " x " << i << " = " << n * i << endl;` 3. The `x` inside the quotes is just text; the real multiplication is `n * i`. 4. With `i < 10` the last row is missing (off-by-one).

problems.title: Sum and average
problems.description:
# Lecture 02 · Homework 03 · Sum and average ## Task Read N, then N whole numbers into an array. Print their sum and their average with exactly 2 decimals. ## Input The first line contains N (1 to 100). The second line contains N whole numbers. ## Output Two lines: `Sum: S` and `Average: A`, where A is printed with 2 decimals. ## Example | Input | Output | |---|---| | `4`
`3 8 1 6` | `Sum: 18`
`Average: 4.50` | | `3`
`-1 -2 -2` | `Sum: -5`
`Average: -1.67` | ## Hints 1. Declare `const int MAX = 100;` and `int a[MAX];`, then use only the first `n` cells. 2. The sum must start at 0: `int sum = 0;` and grows with `sum += a[i];` 3. `sum / n` with two `int` values drops the decimals. Write `(double)sum / n`. 4. `cout << fixed << setprecision(2);` (from ``) prints exactly 2 decimals.

problems.title: Min and max with positions
problems.description:
# Lecture 02 · Homework 04 · Min and max with positions ## Task Read N whole numbers into an array. Print the smallest and the largest value together with their indices (counting from 0). If the smallest or the largest value appears more than once, print the index of its **first** appearance. ## Input The first line contains N (1 to 100). The second line contains N whole numbers. ## Output Two lines: `min VALUE at INDEX` and `max VALUE at INDEX`. ## Example | Input | Output | |---|---| | `5`
`4 -2 9 0 9` | `min -2 at 1`
`max 9 at 2` | | `1`
`42` | `min 42 at 0`
`max 42 at 0` | ## Hints 1. Remember positions: `int minPos = 0, maxPos = 0;` The values are `a[minPos]` and `a[maxPos]`. 2. Start the loop at `i = 1`, because cell 0 is already your first candidate. 3. Use strict `<` and `>` so that ties keep the first index. 4. Compare values with values: `a[i] < a[minPos]`, not `a[i] < minPos`.

problems.title: Reverse an array in place
problems.description:
# Lecture 02 · Homework 05 · Reverse an array in place ## Task Read N whole numbers into an array and reverse the array **in place**: swap elements inside the same array, without using a second array. Then print the array. ## Input The first line contains N (1 to 100). The second line contains N whole numbers. ## Output One line: the elements of the reversed array, separated by spaces. ## Example | Input | Output | |---|---| | `5`
`1 2 3 4 5` | `5 4 3 2 1` | | `6`
`10 20 30 40 50 60` | `60 50 40 30 20 10` | ## Hints 1. The mirror of index `i` is `j = n - 1 - i`. 2. Swap in three steps: `temp = a[i]; a[i] = a[j]; a[j] = temp;` 3. Loop only while `i < n / 2`. If you go to `n`, every pair is swapped twice and the array does not change.

problems.title: Count evens, odds and zeros
problems.description:
# Lecture 02 · Homework 06 · Count evens, odds and zeros ## Task Read N whole numbers into an array. Count how many of them are even, how many are odd and how many are zero. Zero counts as even **and** as zero. ## Input The first line contains N (1 to 100). The second line contains N whole numbers (they can be negative). ## Output Three lines: `even E`, `odd O` and `zero Z`. ## Example | Input | Output | |---|---| | `6`
`0 3 8 5 2 0` | `even 4`
`odd 2`
`zero 2` | | `5`
`-3 -4 7 1 9` | `even 1`
`odd 4`
`zero 0` | ## Hints 1. Three counters, all starting at 0: `int even = 0, odd = 0, zero = 0;` 2. A number is even when `a[i] % 2 == 0`. Do not test `== 1` for odd: `-3 % 2` is `-1`. 3. The zero test is a **separate** `if`, not an `else if`, otherwise zeros are never counted.

problems.title: Split into two halves
problems.description:
# Lecture 02 · Homework 07 · Split into two halves ## Task Read an even number N and N whole numbers. Split the array into two sub-arrays of length N/2: `left` gets the first half, `right` gets the second half. Print the sum of each half and which half is larger. ## Input The first line contains an even N (2 to 100). The second line contains N whole numbers. ## Output Three lines: `left SUM_LEFT`, `right SUM_RIGHT`, and then `left is larger`, `right is larger` or `equal`. ## Example | Input | Output | |---|---| | `6`
`1 2 3 10 20 30` | `left 6`
`right 60`
`right is larger` | | `2`
`5 5` | `left 5`
`right 5`
`equal` | ## Hints 1. `int h = n / 2;` is the length of one half. 2. In one loop `for (int i = 0; i < h; i++)`: `left[i] = a[i];` and `right[i] = a[i + h];` 3. The sums can be computed in the same loop. 4. Loop to `h`, not to `n`: `a[i + h]` with `i >= h` is outside the array.

problems.title: Is it a palindrome array?
problems.description:
# Lecture 02 · Homework 08 · Is it a palindrome array? ## Task Read N whole numbers into an array. Print `YES` if the array reads the same forwards and backwards (a palindrome), otherwise print `NO`. ## Input The first line contains N (1 to 100). The second line contains N whole numbers. ## Output One line: `YES` or `NO`. ## Example | Input | Output | |---|---| | `5`
`1 4 7 5 1` | `NO` | | `5`
`1 4 7 4 1` | `YES` | ## Hints 1. Start with `bool pal = true;` and look for a pair that proves the opposite. 2. Compare `a[i]` with its mirror `a[n - 1 - i]` for `i < n / 2`. The middle element (odd N) needs no partner. 3. When a pair differs, set `pal = false;` and leave the loop with `break;` 4. `a[n - i]` is off by one: for `i = 0` it is outside the array.

problems.title: Rotate right by one
problems.description:
# Lecture 02 · Homework 09 · Rotate right by one ## Task Read N whole numbers into an array and rotate the array one position to the right: every element moves one cell to the right and the last element moves to the front. Then print the array. ## Input The first line contains N (1 to 100). The second line contains N whole numbers. ## Output One line: the rotated array, elements separated by spaces. ## Example | Input | Output | |---|---| | `5`
`1 2 3 4 5` | `5 1 2 3 4` | | `3`
`-1 0 8` | `8 -1 0` | ## Hints 1. Save the last element first: `int last = a[n - 1];` 2. Shift with a reverse loop: `for (int i = n - 1; i >= 1; i--) a[i] = a[i - 1];` 3. Finally `a[0] = last;` 4. A forward loop (`i = 1` up to `n - 1`) overwrites values before they are moved and gives `1 1 1 1 1`.

problems.title: Running (prefix) sums
problems.description:
# Lecture 02 · Homework 10 · Running (prefix) sums ## Task Read N whole numbers into an array `a`. Build a second array `p` where `p[i]` is the sum `a[0] + a[1] + ... + a[i]`. Print `p`. ## Input The first line contains N (1 to 100). The second line contains N whole numbers. ## Output One line: the N elements of `p`, separated by spaces. ## Example | Input | Output | |---|---| | `5`
`3 1 4 1 5` | `3 4 8 9 14` | | `4`
`2 -2 2 -2` | `2 0 2 0` | ## Hints 1. The first element is special: `p[0] = a[0];` 2. Then `for (int i = 1; i < n; i++) p[i] = p[i - 1] + a[i];` Each total reuses the previous one. 3. # Lecture 02 · Homework 13 · Row and column sums

## Task

Read the size of a matrix and the matrix itself. Print the sum of every row and the sum of every column.

First line: `R C` (1 ≤ R, C ≤ 100). Then R lines with C whole numbers each.

## Output

Two lines: `rows:` followed by the R row sums, and `cols:` followed by the C column sums, separated by spaces.

| `1 1` / `7` | `rows: 7` / `cols: 7` |

## Hints

1. Row sums: outer loop over `i` (rows), inner loop over `j` (columns).
2. Column sums: swap the loops, the inner line `sum += m[i][j];` stays the same.

problems.description:
# Lecture 02 · Homework 14 · Diagonals of a square matrix

## Task

Read N and an N × N matrix. Print the sum of the main diagonal (top-left to bottom-right) and the sum of the secondary diagonal (top-right to bottom-left).

## Input

First line: `N` (1 ≤ N ≤ 100). Then N lines with N whole numbers each.

`main A, secondary B`

|---|---|
| `3` / `1 2 3` / `4 5 6` / `7 8 9` | `main 15, secondary 15` |
| `1` / `5` | `main 5, secondary 5` |

1. On the main diagonal the row equals the column: `m[i][i]`.
2. On the secondary diagonal `i + j == n - 1`, so the cell is `m[i][n - 1 - i]`.
3. One `for` loop over `i` is enough for both sums.

problems.description:
# Lecture 04 · Homework 02 · Swap with references ## Task Write two functions that swap two whole numbers with a `temp` variable: ```cpp void swapByValue(int a, int b); void swapByRef(int &a, int &b); ``` Read `x` and `y`. Call `swapByValue(x, y)` and print `x` and `y`. Then call `swapByRef(x, y)` and print them again. Explain the difference. ## Input One line with two whole numbers `x y`. ## Output Two lines, exactly in the format of the example. ## Example | Input | Output | |---|---| | `3 8` | `after swapByValue: 3 8`
`after swapByRef: 8 3` | ## Hints 1. The swap itself is the same in both: `temp = a; a = b; b = temp;` 2. Without `&`, the parameters are copies: the swap happens on the copies and they disappear when the function ends. 3. With `&`, `a` and `b` are other names for `x` and `y`. You cannot call `swapByRef(3, 8)`: a reference needs a variable.

# Lecture 04 · Homework 03 · Default-parameter line printer ## Task Write the function ```cpp void line(int length = 10, char symbol = '-', bool newLine = true); ``` It prints `symbol` exactly `length` times, and then a new line, but only if `newLine` is `true`. Read a whole number `n` and a character `c`. Then make these five calls, in this order: ```cpp line(); line(n); line(n, c); line(3, c, false); line(2, '#'); ``` ## Input One line with a whole number `n` (1 to 50) and a character `c`. ## Output Four lines (the fourth call does not end its line, so the fifth call continues it). ## Example | Input | Output | |---|---| | `5 *` | `----------`
`-----`
`*****`
`***##` | ## Hints 1. Default values are written in the signature: `int length = 10`. 2. Arguments fill the parameters from the left. Missing ones at the right end take their defaults. 3. You cannot skip an argument in the middle: `line(, '*')` does not compile.

problems.description:
# Lecture 04 · Homework 04 · Argument or parameter? ## Task Write a program with these three functions: ```cpp int square(int x); // returns x * x void addBonus(int &points, int bonus); // adds bonus to points void printScore(string name, int points); // prints "name: points" ``` In `main`, read a player name, a score and a bonus `extra`. Then call: ```cpp printScore(player, score); addBonus(score, extra); printScore(player, score); printScore("bonus squared", square(extra)); ``` Before you run it: list every **parameter** (in a definition) and every **argument** (in a call), and predict the output. Then remove the `&` in `addBonus` and predict again. ## Input One line: a name (one word), a whole number `score` and a whole number `extra`. ## Output Three lines, exactly in the format of the example. ## Example | Input | Output | |---|---| | `Ana 10 5` | `Ana: 10`
`Ana: 15`
`bonus squared: 25` | ## Hints 1. Parameter = the variable in the function header. Argument = what is written in the call. 2. Arguments go into parameters by position, not by name. A number, a text or another call can also be an argument. 3. Without `&`, `addBonus` adds the bonus to a copy, and the second line would still show `Ana: 10`.

problems.description:
# Lecture 04 · Homework 05 · Balanced brackets

## Task

Read a string made only of the brackets `( ) [ ] { }`. Print `YES` if every bracket is closed by its partner in the right order, otherwise print `NO`. Use a stack.

## Input

One line: a string of brackets without spaces (1 to 1000 characters).

## Output

`YES` or `NO`.

## Example

| Input | Output |
|---|---|
| `{[()]}` | `YES` |
| `([)]` | `NO` |
| `((` | `NO` |

## Hints

1. Opening bracket: `st.push(c)`.
2. Closing bracket: if the stack is empty, or `st.top()` is not its partner, the answer is `NO`. Otherwise `st.pop()`.
3. At the end the stack must be empty. Do not just `return true`: `((` would give `YES`.

problems.description:
# Lecture 04 · Homework 06 · Reverse a word with a stack ## Task Read one word and print it reversed using a stack of `char`. Do it twice: first with `std::stack`, then with your own stack built on a `char` array and an index `top`. ## Input One word (1 to 100 characters, no spaces). ## Output Two lines, both with the reversed word (one from each version). ## Example | Input | Output | |---|---| | `stack` | `kcats`
`kcats` | ## Hints 1. Push every letter, then pop until the stack is empty, printing each `top()`. 2. Array stack: start with `top = -1` (empty). Push: `top++; a[top] = c;`. Pop: `top--`. 3. The second loop runs `while (top >= 0)`. With `top > 0` the first letter is lost.

problems.title: Decimal to binary with a stack
problems.description:
# Lecture 04 · Homework 07 · Decimal to binary with a stack

## Task

Read a positive whole number `n` and print it in binary. While `n > 0`, push `n % 2` on a stack and divide `n` by 2. Then pop everything and print it.

## Input

One positive whole number `n` (1 to 1 000 000 000).

## Output

One line: `n` in binary, without leading zeros.

## Example

| Input | Output |
|---|---|
| `13` | `1101` |
| `255` | `11111111` |

## Hints

1. `n % 2` is the last bit of `n`, and `n /= 2` removes it.
2. The remainders appear from the last bit to the first. A stack gives them back in the opposite order.
3. Do not print the remainders inside the first loop: `13` would print `1011`.

problems.title: Remove 103, generalised
problems.description:
# Lecture 04 · Homework 08 · Remove 103, generalised

## Task

Extend the lecture solution for "remove 103". Read a digit string `s` and a pattern `p` (for example `42`). Keep removing the pattern from `s` until it does not appear any more. Print what is left, or `(empty)` if nothing is left.

## Input

One line: the digit string `s` (1 to 1000 digits) and the pattern `p` (1 to 10 digits), separated by a space.

## Output

One line: the remaining digits, or `(empty)`.

## Example

| Input | Output |
|---|---|
| `14422 42` | `1` |
| `444222 42` | `(empty)` |
| `241103031 103` | `241` |

## Hints

1. Push the digits one by one. After each push, check if the top `k` chars (`k` = length of `p`) spell `p`.
2. The top `k` chars, from bottom to top, are `st[top - k + 1]` ... `st[top]`. If there are fewer than `k` chars, there is no match.
3. On a match, pop all of them at once with `top -= k`. A removal can bring a new match together, and the stack handles that by itself.

problems.title: Stack with min in O(1)
problems.description:
# Lecture 04 · Homework 09 · Stack with min in O(1) ## Task Implement an array stack with three functions: ```cpp void push(int x); void pop(); int getMin(); // the smallest element in the stack, instantly ``` `getMin()` must not search the stack. Keep a second array: `minAt[i]` = the minimum of `val[0..i]`. Read N numbers and push them all. Print the minimum. Then, while more than one element is left, pop one and print the minimum again. ## Input The first line contains N (1 to 100). The second line contains N whole numbers. ## Output N lines of the form `min: X`. ## Example | Input | Output | |---|---| | `4`
`5 3 7 2` | `min: 2`
`min: 3`
`min: 3`
`min: 5` | ## Hints 1. On push: if the stack was empty, or `x < minAt[top - 1]`, then `minAt[top] = x`, otherwise `minAt[top] = minAt[top - 1]`. 2. `pop()` is just `top--`, and `getMin()` is just `return minAt[top];` 3. A single `min` variable is not enough: after popping the minimum, you would not know the previous one.

problems.title: Point and rectangle structs
problems.description:
# Lecture 04 · Homework 15 · Point and rectangle structs ## Task Define ```cpp struct Point { double x, y; }; struct Rect { Point topLeft, bottomRight; }; ``` and write the functions ```cpp double distance(Point a, Point b); // distance between two points double area(Rect r); // area of the rectangle bool contains(Rect r, Point p); // is p inside r (or on its border)? ``` Read a rectangle (its top-left and bottom-right corner) and a point. Print the area, whether the rectangle contains the point, and the length of the rectangle's diagonal. ## Input The first line contains four numbers: `topLeft.x topLeft.y bottomRight.x bottomRight.y`. The second line contains the point `x y`. ## Output Three lines, exactly in the format of the example. ## Example | Input | Output | |---|---| | `0 4 5 0`
`2 1` | `area: 20`
`contains: yes`
`diagonal: 6.40312` | ## Hints 1. Chain the dots to reach a coordinate: `r.topLeft.x`, `r.bottomRight.y`. 2. The top has the bigger y: height = `r.topLeft.y - r.bottomRight.y`. The other way round gives a negative area. 3. `contains` is four comparisons joined with `&&`. The diagonal is `distance(r.topLeft, r.bottomRight)`.

problems.title: Fraction calculator
problems.description:
# Lecture 04 · Homework 16 · Fraction calculator ## Task Define `struct Fraction { int num, den; };` and write: ```cpp int gcd(int a, int b); // greatest common divisor Fraction simplify(Fraction f); // divide num and den by the gcd Fraction add(Fraction a, Fraction b); // simplified sum Fraction multiply(Fraction a, Fraction b); // simplified product ``` Read two fractions and print their sum and product, simplified. ## Input One line with two positive fractions written as `num/den`, for example `1/2 1/6`. ## Output Two lines, exactly in the format of the example. ## Example | Input | Output | |---|---| | `1/2 1/6` | `sum: 2/3`
`product: 1/12` | | `1/2 1/3` | `sum: 5/6`
`product: 1/6` | ## Hints 1. a/b + c/d = (a·d + c·b) / (b·d), and a/b · c/d = (a·c) / (b·d). 2. gcd: while `b != 0`, do `r = a % b; a = b; b = r;`. At the end, `a` is the gcd. 3. Read the `/` into a `char` variable. Do not add the numerators and the denominators separately: `1/2 + 1/6` is not `2/8`.

problems.title: Linked list builder
problems.description:
# Lecture 04 · Homework 17 · Linked list builder ## Task Use ```cpp struct Node { int value; Node* next; }; ``` and an array `Node pool[10]` as storage. Read N numbers, put each one into the next node of the pool and **link** the nodes in the order they were read. The last node's `next` is `nullptr`. Then walk the list by following the pointers (not the array indices). Print the list, its length and its sum. ## Input The first line contains N (1 to 10). The second line contains N whole numbers. ## Output Two lines, exactly in the format of the example. ## Example | Input | Output | |---|---| | `4`
`7 2 9 5` | `7 -> 2 -> 9 -> 5 -> nullptr`
`length 4, sum 23` | ## Hints 1. Keep `Node* head` (the first node) and `Node* last` (the last node so far). Both start as `nullptr`. 2. For each new node: set `next = nullptr`. If the list is empty, `head` points to it, otherwise `last->next = &pool[i];`. Then `last = &pool[i];` 3. Walk: `for (Node* p = head; p != nullptr; p = p->next)`. Without `next = nullptr` on the last node, this loop never stops safely.

problems.title: Insert and delete in a linked list
problems.description:
# Lecture 04 · Homework 18 · Insert and delete in a linked list ## Task Build the list `10 -> 20 -> 30` from three local `Node` variables (as in the lecture). Write: ```cpp void insertAfter(Node* p, Node* newNode); // put newNode right after p void deleteAfter(Node* p); // remove the node after p void printList(Node* head); ``` Read two values `v1` and `v2` and put them into two new nodes. Then: insert `v1` after 10, insert `v2` after 30, delete the node after 20. Print the list after each of the three steps. ## Input One line with two whole numbers `v1 v2`. ## Output Three lines: the list after each step. ## Example | Input | Output | |---|---| | `15 35` | `10 15 20 30`
`10 15 20 30 35`
`10 15 20 35` | ## Hints 1. Insert in two steps, in this order: `newNode->next = p->next;` then `p->next = newNode;` 2. The other order loses the rest of the list: the new node ends up pointing to itself. 3. Delete: `p->next = p->next->next;` (check first that `p->next` is not `nullptr`).

problems.title: Binary tree measurements
problems.description:
# Lecture 04 · Homework 19 · Binary tree measurements ## Task Using the lecture's `TreeNode { int value; TreeNode* left; TreeNode* right; }`, write recursive functions: ```cpp int sum(TreeNode* t); // sum of all values int height(TreeNode* t); // number of levels (empty tree: 0) int countLeaves(TreeNode* t); // nodes with no children int maxValue(TreeNode* t); // the biggest value ``` Read six values and build a tree with the same shape as the lecture tree: node 0 is the root, nodes 1 and 2 are its children, nodes 3 and 4 are the children of node 1, and node 5 is the right child of node 2. Print all four results. ## Input One line with six whole numbers (the lecture tree is `8 3 10 1 6 14`). ## Output Four lines, exactly in the format of the example. ## Example | Input | Output | |---|---| | `8 3 10 1 6 14` | `sum 42`
`height 3`
`leaves 3`
`max 14` | ## Hints 1. Start every function with the base case: `if (t == nullptr) return 0;` 2. `height` is `1 + max(height(left), height(right))`. A leaf has height 1. 3. For `maxValue`, start with `t->value` and only visit children that are not `nullptr`.

problems.title: Binary search tree insert
problems.description:
# Lecture 04 · Homework 20 · Binary search tree insert ## Task Use the lecture's `TreeNode` and an array `TreeNode pool[100]` as storage. Write: ```cpp TreeNode* insert(TreeNode* t, int value); // returns the (new) root of this subtree void printInOrder(TreeNode* t); // left, node, right void search(TreeNode* t, int value); // prints the path and the result ``` `insert` walks left (smaller) or right (bigger or equal) until it finds an empty spot (`nullptr`) and hangs a new node from the pool there. Read N values and insert them in order, starting from an empty tree. Print the tree in order (it should be sorted). Then read two values and search for each one, printing the nodes visited. ## Input The first line contains N (1 to 100), the second line N whole numbers, the third line the two values to search for. ## Output `in order:` and the sorted values, then one `search` line for each of the two values. ## Example | Input | Output | |---|---| | `7`
`50 30 70 20 40 60 80`
`60 65` | `in order: 20 30 40 50 60 70 80`
`search 60: 50 70 60 found`
`search 65: 50 70 60 not found` | ## Hints 1. In `insert`: if `t == nullptr`, take `&pool[used]`, fill it, `used++`, and return it. 2. Otherwise `t->left = insert(t->left, value);` (or right). Without `t->left =`, the new node is lost. 3. In-order printing of a BST always gives the values sorted. A search checks only one node per level.

tests.output:
in order: 20 30 40 50 60 70 80
search 60: 50 70 60 found
search 65: 50 70 60 not found

in order: 1 2 3 4 8
search 3: 4 2 3 found
search 9: 4 8 not found

in order: 1 2 3 4
search 4: 1 2 3 4 found
search 0: 1 not found

problems.title: Bubble sort with a counter
problems.description:
# Lecture 05 · Homework 01 · Bubble sort with a counter ## Task Read N numbers and sort them with bubble sort. Count every comparison of two neighbours and every swap. Stop early as soon as a pass makes no swaps. Print the sorted array, the number of comparisons and the number of swaps. ## Input The first line contains N (1 to 100). The second line contains N whole numbers. ## Output Two lines: the sorted array, then `comparisons X, swaps Y`. ## Example | Input | Output | |---|---| | `5`
`3 1 2 5 4` | `1 2 3 4 5`
`comparisons 7, swaps 3` | ## Hints 1. `comparisons++` goes before the `if`, so every check is counted, swap or not. 2. `swaps++` goes inside the `if`, next to the swap itself. 3. Set `bool swapped = false;` at the start of every pass. If it is still `false` after the pass, `break`.

problems.title: Descending bubble sort
problems.description:
# Lecture 05 · Homework 02 · Descending bubble sort ## Task Take the lecture's bubble sort (with the early stop) and change it so it sorts from largest to smallest. Change only **one character** in the code, and explain which one and why. Print the array after every pass. ## Input The first line contains N (2 to 100). The second line contains N whole numbers. ## Output One line per pass: `after pass K:` followed by the array. ## Example | Input | Output | |---|---| | `5`
`5 1 4 2 8` | `after pass 1: 5 4 2 8 1`
`after pass 2: 5 4 8 2 1`
`after pass 3: 5 8 4 2 1`
`after pass 4: 8 5 4 2 1` | ## Hints 1. The comparison `a[i] > a[i + 1]` decides when two neighbours are in the wrong order. 2. With `a[i] < a[i + 1]`, the smallest value bubbles to the end in every pass. 3. Use `<`, not `<=`: equal neighbours must not be swapped, or the early stop never happens.

tests.output:
after pass 1: 5 4 2 8 1
after pass 2: 5 4 8 2 1
after pass 3: 5 8 4 2 1
after pass 4: 8 5 4 2 1

after pass 1: 3 3 6 1
after pass 2: 3 6 3 1
after pass 3: 6 3 3 1

problems.title: Selection sort
problems.description:
# Lecture 05 · Homework 03 · Selection sort ## Task Implement selection sort: for each position `i`, find the minimum of `a[i..N-1]` and swap it into position `i`. Do not swap a value with itself. Count the swaps. Compare with bubble sort: bubble sort makes exactly one swap for every pair `i < j` with `a[i] > a[j]`. Count those pairs before sorting and print both numbers. ## Input The first line contains N (1 to 100). The second line contains N whole numbers. ## Output Two lines: the sorted array, then `selection swaps X, bubble swaps Y`. ## Example | Input | Output | |---|---| | `5`
`64 25 12 22 11` | `11 12 22 25 64`
`selection swaps 3, bubble swaps 9` | ## Hints 1. Keep `minIdx`, the **index** of the smallest value so far, not only the value itself. 2. After the inner loop, swap `a[i]` and `a[minIdx]`, but only if `minIdx != i`. 3. Selection sort makes at most N - 1 swaps. Bubble sort can make many more.

problems.title: Sort by absolute value
problems.description:
# Lecture 05 · Homework 04 · Sort by absolute value ## Task Read N integers and sort them by absolute value (distance from zero) using `std::sort` and your own comparator function. If two numbers have the same absolute value, the negative one comes first. ## Input The first line contains N (1 to 100). The second line contains N integers. ## Output One line: the sorted numbers, separated by spaces. ## Example | Input | Output | |---|---| | `5`
`-7 3 -2 2 5` | `-2 2 3 5 -7` | ## Hints 1. The comparator `bool byAbs(int a, int b)` returns `true` when `a` must come before `b`. 2. If `abs(a) != abs(b)`, return `abs(a) < abs(b)`. Otherwise return `a < b` (the negative one first). 3. Call `sort(a, a + n, byAbs);`, with the function's name and no brackets. Without the tie rule, `-2` and `2` may come out in either order.

problems.title: Words by length, then alphabet
problems.description:
# Lecture 05 · Homework 05 · Words by length, then alphabet ## Task Read N words and sort them with `std::sort` and your own comparator: shorter words first; words of equal length in alphabetical order. ## Input The first line contains N (1 to 100). The second line contains N words (lowercase letters only). ## Output One line: the sorted words, separated by spaces. ## Example | Input | Output | |---|---| | `5`
`pear fig apple kiwi banana` | `fig kiwi pear apple banana` | ## Hints 1. Rule 1: if `a.size() != b.size()`, return `a.size() < b.size()`. 2. Rule 2: otherwise return `a < b`. For strings, `<` compares letter by letter, which gives alphabetical order. 3. `a < b` on its own is not enough: it ignores the lengths.

problems.title: Leaderboard
problems.description:
# Lecture 05 · Homework 06 · Leaderboard ## Task Define `struct Player { string name; int points; int time; };`. Read N players and sort them: 1. more points first, 2. with equal points: less time first, 3. with equal points and time: alphabetically by name. Print a ranked table with positions 1, 2, 3, ... ## Input The first line contains N (1 to 100). Each of the next N lines contains a name (one word), the points and the time. ## Output N lines of the form `K. name points time`. ## Example | Input | Output | |---|---| | `3`
`Ana 90 30`
`Marko 90 25`
`Ivana 70 20` | `1. Marko 90 25`
`2. Ana 90 30`
`3. Ivana 70 20` | ## Hints 1. Check the levels in order: `if (a.points != b.points) return a.points > b.points;` then the same for time, then `return a.name < b.name;` 2. For points "more is better" (`>`); for time "less is better" (`<`). 3. After sorting, the position of `p[i]` is `i + 1`.

problems.title: Linear search: all positions
problems.description:
# Lecture 05 · Homework 07 · Linear search: all positions ## Task Read N numbers and a target. Print every index where the target appears (in increasing order), or `not found`. Also print how many elements you checked. ## Input The first line contains N (1 to 100), the second line N whole numbers, the third line the target. ## Output Two lines: the indices separated by spaces (or `not found`), then `checked X`. ## Example | Input | Output | |---|---| | `7`
`4 2 4 9 4 1 0`
`4` | `0 2 4`
`checked 7` | ## Hints 1. Count every check with `checked++`, match or not. 2. On a match print `i`, set `found = true` and keep going. Do not `break`: there may be more matches. 3. After the loop, `if (!found)` print `not found`.

problems.title: Binary search: first occurrence
problems.description:
# Lecture 05 · Homework 08 · Binary search: first occurrence ## Task Read a sorted array that may contain duplicates, and a target. Using binary search, find the **first** index where the target appears. When you find the target, remember the index and keep searching to the left. ## Input The first line contains N (1 to 100), the second line N whole numbers in non-decreasing order, the third line the target. ## Output `first index X`, or `not found`. ## Example | Input | Output | |---|---| | `6`
`1 2 2 2 3 5`
`2` | `first index 1` | ## Hints 1. Start with `lo = 0`, `hi = n - 1`, `answer = -1`. 2. If `a[mid] == target`: `answer = mid;` and `hi = mid - 1;` (an earlier copy may be on the left). 3. Returning `mid` at the first match, as in the lecture, finds *a* copy, but not always the first one.

problems.title: Guess my number, computer edition
problems.description:
# Lecture 05 · Homework 09 · Guess my number, computer edition ## Task The user picks a secret number from 1 to 1000. The program guesses it with binary search: it prints `guess X`, then reads the user's answer: - `higher`: the secret is bigger than X, - `lower`: the secret is smaller than X, - `yes`: X is the secret. When the answer is `yes`, print `found X in K guesses`. The program never needs more than 10 guesses. ## Input The user's answers, separated by spaces or new lines (in the tests, the answers for a fixed secret). ## Output One `guess X` line per guess, then the `found` line. ## Example Secret 625: | Input | Output | |---|---| | `higher lower yes` | `guess 500`
`guess 750`
`guess 625`
`found 625 in 3 guesses` | ## Hints 1. Start with `lo = 1`, `hi = 1000`. Always guess `(lo + hi) / 2`. 2. `higher`: `lo = guess + 1`. `lower`: `hi = guess - 1`. Without the `+ 1` / `- 1` the range can stop shrinking. 3. Every answer halves the range, and 2^10 = 1024 ≥ 1000, so at most 10 guesses are needed.

problems.title: Integer square root
problems.description:
# Lecture 05 · Homework 10 · Integer square root

## Task

Read n (0 to 10^12) and print the largest whole number x with `x * x <= n`. Do not use `sqrt`: use binary search on x. Use `long long`.

## Input

One whole number n.

## Output

One whole number: the integer square root of n.

## Example

| Input | Output |
|---|---|
| `26` | `5` |
| `1000000000000` | `1000000` |

## Hints

1. The answer is between 0 and n, and never above 1 000 000 (because 1 000 000² = 10^12).
2. If `mid * mid <= n`, mid fits: `ans = mid; lo = mid + 1;`. Otherwise `hi = mid - 1;`.
3. `mid * mid` can be as big as 10^12, much more than an `int` can hold. Make `lo`, `hi`, `mid` and `ans` `long long`.

problems.title: Step race: linear vs binary
problems.description:
# Lecture 05 · Homework 11 · Step race: linear vs binary ## Task Read N and fill a sorted array of size N with `a[i] = 3 * i`. Then read Q queries. For each query, count how many elements linear search and binary search look at before they find the target (or give up). Print both numbers for every query, and the totals at the end. ## Input The first line contains N (1 to 100000), the second line Q, the third line Q whole numbers (the queries). ## Output One line per query: `t: linear X, binary Y`, then `total: linear X, binary Y`. ## Example | Input | Output | |---|---| | `10`
`2`
`27 12` | `27: linear 10, binary 4`
`12: linear 5, binary 1`
`total: linear 15, binary 5` | | `100000`
`1`
`299997` | `299997: linear 100000, binary 17`
`total: linear 100000, binary 17` | ## Hints 1. One step = looking at one element. Put `steps++` right before the comparison. 2. Linear search stops (`break`) as soon as it finds the target. 3. Binary search needs about log2(N) steps: 2^17 = 131072, so 17 steps are enough for 100000 numbers.

tests.output:
27: linear 10, binary 4
12: linear 5, binary 1
total: linear 15, binary 5

0: linear 1, binary 9
1500: linear 501, binary 9
4: linear 1000, binary 10
total: linear 1502, binary 28

problems.title: Unique words
problems.description:
# Lecture 05 · Homework 12 · Unique words

## Task

Read words until the word `end`. Print how many different words there were, and list them in alphabetical order.

## Input

Words separated by spaces or new lines, ending with `end` (which is not counted).

## Output

One line: the number of different words, a colon, and the words in alphabetical order.

## Example

| Input | Output |
|---|---|
| `the cat saw the dog and the cat end` | `5: and cat dog saw the` |

## Hints

1. `words.insert(w)` adds a word; if it is already in the set, nothing happens.
2. `words.size()` is the number of different words. Counting every word you read would include the repeats.
3. A set is always sorted: `for (string x : words)` visits the words alphabetically.

tests.input: the cat saw the dog and the cat end

b a b a c
c end

problems.title: Common elements of two arrays
problems.description:
# Lecture 05 · Homework 13 · Common elements of two arrays ## Task Read two arrays A and B (they may contain repeats). Print the values that appear in both arrays (each value once, sorted), and the values that appear in exactly one of them (sorted). ## Input The first line contains N, the second line N whole numbers (array A). The third line contains M, the fourth line M whole numbers (array B). ## Output Two lines: `common:` followed by the shared values, then `only one:` followed by the other values. ## Example | Input | Output | |---|---| | `5`
`1 4 4 7 9`
`4`
`4 9 9 2` | `common: 4 9`
`only one: 1 2 7` | ## Hints 1. Insert both arrays into `set A, B`: repeats disappear and the values are sorted. 2. Common: loop over the set A and print every `v` with `B.count(v) == 1`. Looping over the original array would print 4 twice. 3. Only one: collect A-without-B and B-without-A in a third set, so they come out sorted together.

problems.title: First repeated value
problems.description:
# Lecture 05 · Homework 14 · First repeated value ## Task Read N numbers. Scanning from left to right, print the first number that appears for the second time. If no number repeats, print `none`. ## Input The first line contains N (1 to 100000). The second line contains N whole numbers. ## Output The first repeated number, or `none`. ## Example | Input | Output | |---|---| | `5`
`5 3 8 3 5` | `3` | ## Hints 1. Keep a `set seen` with every value read so far. 2. For each number: first check `seen.count(x) == 1`; only then `seen.insert(x)`. In the other order, every number looks like a repeat. 3. The first hit is the answer: print it and stop. If the loop ends without a hit, print `none`.

problems.title: Phone book
problems.description:
# Lecture 05 · Homework 15 · Phone book ## Task Read commands until the input ends: - `add NAME NUMBER`: store the number for that name (a second `add` for the same name updates it), - `find NAME`: print the number, or `not found`, - `remove NAME`: delete the entry, - `list`: print every entry as `NAME NUMBER`, sorted by name. Use `map`. In `find`, use `count` first, so you do not create empty entries. ## Input Commands separated by spaces or new lines. ## Output One line for every successful `find`, every `not found`, and every entry printed by `list`. ## Example | Input | Output | |---|---| | `add Ana 070111 add Marko 071222`
`find Ana find Bob`
`remove Ana list` | `070111`
`not found`
`Marko 071222` | ## Hints 1. `book[name] = number;` inserts a new name or updates an existing one. 2. `if (book.count(name) == 1)` before reading `book[name]`. Reading `book["Bob"]` when there is no Bob creates an empty Bob entry. 3. `for (auto p : book)`: `p.first` is the name, `p.second` the number, in alphabetical order.

tests.input:
add Ana 070111 add Marko 071222
find Ana find Bob
remove Ana list

add Ivo 1 add Ivo 2
find Ivo list

find X remove X list
add Zoe 9 add Eva 8 list

problems.title: Letter frequency
problems.description:
# Lecture 05 · Homework 16 · Letter frequency ## Task Read a whole sentence with `getline`. Count how many times each letter appears, ignoring the difference between capital and small letters, and ignoring everything that is not a letter. Print the counts in alphabetical order, then the most common letter (if there is a tie, the one that comes first in the alphabet). ## Input One line of text. ## Output Two lines: `letter:count` pairs separated by spaces, then `most common: X`. ## Example | Input | Output | |---|---| | `Hello World` | `d:1 e:1 h:1 l:3 o:2 r:1 w:1`
`most common: l` | ## Hints 1. `getline(cin, line)` reads the whole line, spaces included. 2. A capital letter becomes small with `c = c - 'A' + 'a';`. Without this step, `H` and `W` are not counted at all. 3. `freq[c]++` creates the key with 0 the first time. Walking the map gives the letters in alphabetical order; remember the biggest count on the way.

most common: l

o:1 p:1 t:1 z:4

problems.title: Anagram check
problems.description:
# Lecture 05 · Homework 17 · Anagram check ## Task Read two words and decide whether they are anagrams (the same letters, each used the same number of times). Solve it twice: - (a) sort the letters of both words and compare the results, - (b) count the letters of each word in a `map` and compare the two maps. ## Input One line with two words (lowercase letters). ## Output Two lines: `sorting: YES/NO` and `counting: YES/NO`. ## Example | Input | Output | |---|---| | `listen silent` | `sorting: YES`
`counting: YES` | | `abc abd` | `sorting: NO`
`counting: NO` | ## Hints 1. `sort(a.begin(), a.end());` sorts the letters of a string. Anagrams give the same sorted string. 2. Two maps are equal (`fa == fb`) when they have the same keys with the same values. 3. A `set` is not enough: `aab` and `ab` contain the same letters but different counts.

problems.title: Top K most frequent
problems.description:
# Lecture 05 · Homework 18 · Top K most frequent ## Task Read N numbers and K. Count each value with a `map`. Copy the (value, count) pairs into an array of ```cpp struct Item { int value, count; }; ``` sort it by count (more first), ties by value (smaller first), and print the top K items. If there are fewer than K different values, print all of them. ## Input The first line contains N (1 to 100), the second line N whole numbers, the third line K. ## Output At most K lines of the form `value (count)`. ## Example | Input | Output | |---|---| | `10`
`4 1 4 2 1 4 3 2 1 5`
`2` | `1 (3)`
`4 (3)` | ## Hints 1. A map counts easily (`freq[x]++`), but it is sorted by value, not by count. Copy the pairs into the array: `items[m].value = p.first; items[m].count = p.second; m++;` 2. Comparator: `if (a.count != b.count) return a.count > b.count; return a.value < b.value;` 3. Print while `i < k && i < m`: with only `i < k`, you may print items that were never filled.

problems.title: Two-sum with a set
problems.description:
# Lecture 05 · Homework 19 · Two-sum with a set ## Task Read N numbers and a target T. Print `YES (a + b)` if two numbers at **different** positions add up to T (the first pair found in one left-to-right pass), otherwise `NO`. Use one pass: for each x, check whether `T - x` is already in a set, then insert x. ## Input The first line contains N (1 to 100), the second line N whole numbers, the third line T. ## Output `YES (a + b)` or `NO`. ## Example | Input | Output | |---|---| | `4`
`2 7 11 15`
`9` | `YES (2 + 7)` | | `2`
`3 3`
`6` | `YES (3 + 3)` | | `1`
`3`
`6` | `NO` | ## Hints 1. The partner you need for `x` is `need = T - x`. 2. `if (seen.count(need) == 1)` you found a pair. Only after that check, `seen.insert(x)`. 3. Inserting before the check lets a number pair with itself: `3` alone with T = 6 would wrongly give YES.

problems.title: Student grade book
problems.description:
# Lecture 05 · Homework 20 · Student grade book ## Task Read N lines of the form `NAME SUBJECT GRADE`. Use a `map` for the sum of grades per student and another one for the number of grades. Print each student's average with two decimals (sorted by name), then the student with the best average (the first one by name if there is a tie). problems.title: Recursive sum and power
problems.description:
# Lecture 08 · Homework 01 · Recursive sum and power ## Task Write these functions with recursion, without any loops: ```cpp int sumTo(int n); // 1 + 2 + ... + n long long power(int a, int b); // a^b, using power(a, b - 1) int digitSum(int n); // the sum of the digits of n ``` In a comment, name the base case and the recursive case of each function. ## Input Four whole numbers: `n`, then `a b`, then `d` (all not negative). ## Output Three lines, exactly in the format of the example. ## Example | Input | Output | |---|---| | `4`
`2 10`
`4096` | `sumTo(4) = 10`
`power(2, 10) = 1024`
`digitSum(4096) = 19` | ## Hints 1. `sumTo`: base case `n == 0` returns 0; recursive case `n + sumTo(n - 1)`. 2. `power`: base case `b == 0` returns 1; recursive case `a * power(a, b - 1)`. 3. `digitSum`: base case `n < 10` returns n; recursive case `n % 10 + digitSum(n / 10)`. Without a base case the calls never stop and the program crashes.

problems.title: Reverse with recursion
problems.description:
# Lecture 08 · Homework 02 · Reverse with recursion ## Task (a) Print an array in reverse using recursion: `printReverse(i)` first calls `printReverse(i + 1)` and prints `a[i]` after it. (b) Check recursively whether a word is a palindrome: compare the two ends, then check the middle with a recursive call. ## Input The first line contains N (1 to 100), the second line N whole numbers, the third line one word. ## Output Two lines: the array in reverse, then `YES` or `NO`. ## Example | Input | Output | |---|---| | `3`
`1 2 3`
`racecar` | `3 2 1`
`YES` | ## Hints 1. Base case of `printReverse`: `i == n`, there is nothing left to print. 2. Code after the recursive call runs on the way back up, so the values come out in reverse order. 3. `isPal(s, lo, hi)`: base case `lo >= hi` (0 or 1 letters left). `lo == hi` is not enough: for even lengths, lo and hi jump past each other.

problems.title: GCD the recursive way
problems.description:
# Lecture 08 · Homework 03 · GCD the recursive way ## Task Implement `gcd(a, b)` recursively, using `gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a % b)` and `gcd(a, 0) = a`. Every call prints `(a,b) ` so the chain of calls is visible. Then use the gcd to simplify the fraction `a/b`. ## Input One line with two positive whole numbers `a b`. ## Output Three lines: the chain of calls, `gcd X`, and the simplified fraction. ## Example | Input | Output | |---|---| | `48 18` | `(48,18) (18,12) (12,6) (6,0)`
`gcd 6`
`48/18 = 8/3` | ## Hints 1. Base case: `if (b == 0) return a;`. Returning `b` there would give 0. 2. Recursive case: `return gcd(b, a % b);`. The remainder is smaller than `b`, so the calls end quickly. 3. Simplify with `a / g` and `b / g`.

problems.title: Count the calls
problems.description:
# Lecture 08 · Homework 04 · Count the calls ## Task For every n from 1 to N, run the plain recursive `fib(n)` and count how many times the function is called. Then do the same with a memoized version (`memo[]` and `known[]` arrays). Print one line per n: `n fib(n) plainCalls memoCalls`. Look at the plain column and find the pattern: `calls(n) = calls(n-1) + calls(n-2) + 1`. ## Input One whole number N (1 to 30). ## Output A header line `n fib plain memo`, then N lines. ## Example | Input | Output | |---|---| | `6` | `n fib plain memo`
`1 1 1 1`
`2 1 3 3`
`3 2 5 5`
`4 3 9 7`
`5 5 15 9`
`6 8 25 11` | For N = 10 the last line is `10 55 177 19`; for N = 30 it is `30 832040 2692537 59`. ## Hints 1. Use a global `long long calls` and do `calls++` at the start of each function. 2. Memoized: `if (known[n]) return memo[n];` before the recursive calls, store the result after. 3. Before every memoized run, reset `calls = 0` and `known[i] = false`, or the count is wrong.

problems.title: Climbing stairs
problems.description:
# Lecture 08 · Homework 05 · Climbing stairs

## Task

You climb a staircase taking 1 or 2 steps at a time. In how many different ways can you climb N stairs? Solve it recursively, then add memoization so that N = 80 is instant.

## Input

One whole number N (1 to 80).

## Output

The number of ways.

## Example

| Input | Output |
|---|---|
| `4` | `5` |
| `80` | `37889062373143906` |

For N = 4 the ways are 1111, 112, 121, 211 and 22.

## Hints

1. The last move was 1 step (from stair N - 1) or 2 steps (from stair N - 2): `ways(n) = ways(n - 1) + ways(n - 2)`.
2. Base case: `n <= 1` has exactly one way.
3. Store every result in `memo[n]` with `known[n] = true`. The answer for N = 80 does not fit in an `int`: use `long long`.

problems.title: All subsets
problems.description:
# Lecture 08 · Homework 06 · All subsets ## Task Read N different numbers (N ≤ 15) and a target S. Print every subset (for each element, recursively skip it or take it), and at the end how many subsets there are and how many of them have sum S. ## Input The first line contains N, the second line N different whole numbers, the third line S. ## Output One line with every subset in the form `{a b c}`, separated by spaces (the skip branch first), then a line `X subsets, Y with sum S`. ## Example | Input | Output | |---|---| | `3`
`1 2 3`
`3` | `{} {3} {2} {2 3} {1} {1 3} {1 2} {1 2 3}`
`8 subsets, 2 with sum 3` | ## Hints 1. `subsets(i, sum)`: base case `i == n`, print the chosen elements. 2. First `subsets(i + 1, sum)` (skip), then choose `chosen[cnt++] = a[i];`, explore `subsets(i + 1, sum + a[i])`, undo `cnt--`. 3. Without the undo, elements from earlier branches stay in the basket.

problems.title: All permutations
problems.description:
# Lecture 08 · Homework 07 · All permutations ## Task Read N (1 to 8). Print all permutations of the numbers 1..N in lexicographic (sorted) order, one per line, using a `bool used[]` array and backtracking. At the end print how many there were. ## Input One whole number N. ## Output N! lines with one permutation each (digits without spaces), then `total X`. ## Example | Input | Output | |---|---| | `3` | `123`
`132`
`213`
`231`
`312`
`321`
`total 6` | ## Hints 1. `permute(pos)`: base case `pos == n`, print `perm[0..n-1]`. 2. For `x` from 1 to n: skip it if `used[x]`. Otherwise choose (`perm[pos] = x; used[x] = true;`), explore (`permute(pos + 1)`), undo (`used[x] = false;`). 3. Without the undo, numbers stay used forever and you only get the first permutation.

problems.title: Balanced parentheses generator
problems.description:
# Lecture 08 · Homework 08 · Balanced parentheses generator ## Task Read N and print all strings of N pairs of correctly balanced parentheses (in the order produced by trying `(` before `)`). Prune the search: add `(` only if `open < N`, and add `)` only if `close < open`. At the end print how many strings there were. ## Input One whole number N (1 to 8). ## Output One string per line, then `total X`. ## Example | Input | Output | |---|---| | `3` | `((()))`
`(()())`
`(())()`
`()(())`
`()()()`
`total 5` | ## Hints 1. `gen(s, open, close)`: base case `s.size() == 2 * n`, print `s`. 2. `if (open < n) gen(s + "(", open + 1, close);` and `if (close < open) gen(s + ")", open, close + 1);` 3. With `close < n` instead of `close < open`, wrong strings like `())(()` would appear. Out of 2^6 = 64 strings of length 6, only 5 are balanced.

problems.title: Rat in a maze
problems.description:
# Lecture 08 · Homework 10 · Rat in a maze ## Task Read a maze: `.` free cell, `#` wall, `S` start, `E` exit. Find a path from S to E with depth-first search and backtracking, trying the directions in the order down, right, up, left. Mark the path with `*` and print the maze. If there is no path, print `no way out`. ## Input The first line contains R and C (up to 20). Each of the next R lines contains C characters. ## Output The maze with the path marked, or `no way out`. ## Example | Input | Output | |---|---| | `4 4`
`S...`
`.##.`
`.#..`
`##.E` | `S***`
`.##*`
`.#.*`
`##.E` | ## Hints 1. `go(r, c)`: return `false` outside the maze, on a wall or on a cell already `seen`; return `true` on `E`. 2. Choose: `seen[r][c] = true;` and mark a `.` with `*`. Explore the four neighbours and return `true` as soon as one succeeds. 3. On a dead end, undo: turn the `*` back into `.`, but keep `seen`. Without `seen`, the rat walks back and forth forever.

problems.title: Sudoku checker
problems.description:
# Lecture 08 · Homework 11 · Sudoku checker

## Task

Read a filled 9 × 9 Sudoku grid. Check the rows (top to bottom), then the columns (left to right), then the 3 × 3 boxes (left to right, top to bottom). Print `VALID`, or the first rule that is broken, in the form `row 1 has two 4s` (numbers counted from 1).

## Input

9 lines with 9 digits each (1 to 9), separated by spaces.

## Output

`VALID` or one line describing the first problem.

## Example

| Input | Output |
|---|---|
| the lecture's solved grid, with the last digit of row 1 changed to 4 | `row 1 has two 4s` |
| the lecture's solved grid | `VALID` |

## Hints

1. Write one function that checks 9 cells with a fresh `bool seen[10] = {false};`. A digit that is already seen is a repeat.
2. Box `k`, cell `i`: `r = k / 3 * 3 + i / 3`, `c = k % 3 * 3 + i % 3`.
3. If `seen` is global and never reset, even a correct grid reports a repeat.

# Lecture 08 · Homework 14 · Measure it yourself ## Task Measure three functions: a linear sum O(N), bubble sort O(N²) and `std::sort` O(N log N). To get the same result on every computer, count basic steps instead of measuring time: - linear sum: one step per element, - bubble sort (without early stop): one step per comparison, - `std::sort`: one step per call of your own comparator. Print the counts, then the ratio of every row to the previous one. In real life you would measure time with `` (`steady_clock::now()` before and after); the ratios are the same, but noisy. ## Input One line: the first N and the number of rows. ## Output One line per N: `N=...:` followed by the three counts. Then one line per doubling: `2N/N:` followed by the three ratios. ## Example | Input | Output | |---|---| | `1000 4` | `N=1000: 1000 499500 11809`

Print the picture. ## Input R and C, then R lines of C letters, then the start row, start column and the new colour. ## Output The picture after painting. ## Example | Input | Output | |---|---| | `4 5`

`abbba`

`bbaab` | ## Hints 1. Remember `oldC = g[sr][sc]` before painting. 2. `paint(r, c, oldC, newC)`: stop outside the grid or when `g[r][c] != oldC`; otherwise set `g[r][c] = newC` and try the 4 neighbours. Repainting a cell marks it as visited. 3. If `oldC == newC`, do nothing: painted cells would still look unvisited and the recursion would never stop.

# Lecture 08 · Homework 20 · Word search ## Task Read a letter grid and Q words. For each word print YES if it can be built from adjacent cells (up, down, left, right), using each cell at most once in that word, otherwise NO. Use DFS with backtracking: mark a cell as used, try the neighbours for the next letter, and unmark the cell on the way back. ## Input R and C, then R lines of letters, then Q and Q words. ## Output One line per word: `WORD: YES` or `WORD: NO`. ## Example | Input | Output | |---|---| | `3 3`
`CAT`
`XRS`
`DOG`
`3 CAT CATS ROAD` | `CAT: YES`
`CATS: YES`
`ROAD: NO` | ## Hints 1. Try every cell as the start: `match(r, c, 0)`. 2. `match(r, c, k)`: false outside the grid, on a used cell or on a wrong letter; true if `k` is the last index. Otherwise mark `used[r][c] = true`, try the 4 neighbours with `k + 1`, then `used[r][c] = false`. 3. Without the unmark, cells of a failed path stay blocked and a word that is in the grid can get NO.
